content.text: Still working: I've mapped how similar tasks are to each other. Next I'll train on two tasks and test the learner on tasks that separate "known rule parts" from "similar overall mapping".
Results so far are very noisy (from 1 to 42 examples), so I'm collecting more samples of each test.
Early pattern: tasks built from known rules are learned fastest, even when they look dissimilar. I'm adding samples to firm this up.

content.text:
I submitted **part-based** with confidence 0.9, using 38 of the 60 budget.

**Design:** I trained the learner on two tasks, L1-S1-M1 and L2-S2-M4. Then I tested tasks where the two hypotheses predict opposite results. One test task was made entirely of rules the learner already knew but looked unlike anything it was trained on. Others contained new rules but looked more like the trained tasks.

| Test task | New rules | Highest overlap with a trained task | Mean examples to criterion |
|---|---|---|---|
| L1-S1-M4 | 0 | 0.375 | 12.4 (n=14) |
| L1-S1-M3 | 1 | 0.75 | 23.4 (n=14) |
| L1-S3-M3 | 2 | 0.5625 | 35.8 (n=5) |
| L3-S3-M3 | 3 | 0.5625 | 40.3 (n=3) |

**Evidence:**
- **Main result:** L1-S1-M4 had the lowest overlap with training but was learned fastest, about twice as fast as L1-S1-M3, which had the highest overlap. A holistic learner should show the reverse. This is the result the verdict rests on. Its difference is about 2.8 standard errors.
- **Overall pattern:** learning cost rose steadily with the number of new rules.
- **Weaker point:** L1-S3-M3 and L3-S3-M3 have the same overlap with training. L3-S3-M3, which has more new rules, cost a little more. But with only 5 and 3 samples this gap is small and unreliable, so it adds little.

The tests are very noisy: a single task gave anywhere from 1 to 42 examples. That noise is why I didn't set the confidence higher than 0.9.
